passage:
Tushar's diary, Saturday evening. On the school trip today Sumit climbed over the railing of the old canal bridge for a dare. Half the group were filming and shouting his name. He was smiling for the phones, not looking down. My stomach dropped. I shouted, and two of the older boys hauled him back over.
I sent the group to the bus, sat Sumit down with water, checked he was unhurt and rang his mother right there. Later I asked what it was for. "Everyone said I wouldn't," he said.
I thought of the bird-rescue day last year, when he waded in to free a trapped kite and nobody was watching. I wonder which Sumit is the braver one. Monday: speak to the head and the group.

qa.q: Where did Sumit climb over the railing?
qa.a: On the old canal bridge.

qa.q: What did Tushar feel when Sumit went over the railing?
qa.a: Alarm. Tushar's stomach dropped and Tushar shouted.

qa.q: What protective steps did Tushar take?
qa.a: Tushar shouted, had older boys haul Sumit back, sent the group to the bus, checked Sumit was unhurt and rang Sumit's mother at once.

qa.q: How does Sumit explain the climb?
qa.a: Sumit says everyone said he wouldn't, so the dare served an audience, unlike the kite rescue, which nobody watched.

grounding: Adults watch a teenager take a dangerous dare and struggle to tell bravery from need for approval.

passage:
Varun: Did you see Parth on the rocks?
Baljeet: I did. My heart's still going
Varun: Fifteen years old, and he looked at the phones before he looked at the water
Baljeet: Yes. Compare last year, when he pulled the dog out of the current. Nobody filmed that
Varun: True. He was quiet after, just wet
Baljeet: The dare was for the audience. The dog was for the dog 🤔
Varun: I made him climb down and we had a local guide check the pool. No more jumps today
Baljeet: Good. I'll talk to him tomorrow, not in front of his friends
Varun: Ask what he was proving
Baljeet: And to whom

qa.q: What did Parth look at before looking at the water?
qa.a: The phones.

qa.q: What is Baljeet feeling and thinking about Parth's jump?
qa.a: Baljeet is shaken, with a heart still going, and thinks the jump was for an audience, unlike the dog rescue.

qa.q: What protective choice did Varun make, and what does Baljeet plan?
qa.a: Varun made Parth climb down, had a local guide check the pool and ended the jumps for the day. Baljeet plans to talk to Parth tomorrow, away from friends.

qa.q: How might Parth see the rock jump compared with the dog rescue?
qa.a: Probably as very different: one was for friends holding phones, the other was done quietly for the dog, which Parth may see if asked.

grounding: Adults watch a teenager take a dangerous dare and question whether it is bravery or a need for approval.

passage:
On a monsoon afternoon, Mridul was walking back from the fields when he saw a crowd of boys on the old railway bridge over the swollen river. His nephew Pradeep was standing on the wrong side of the railing, and three boys had their phones out, filming. "Jump! Jump!" they chanted.
Mridul's stomach dropped. Pradeep had pulled a drowning goat out of this river last year, calmly, with a rope. This was different. He kept looking at the phones, not the water.
Mridul didn't shout. He walked up quickly and said, "Pradeep, come back over. Now. Give me your hand." Pradeep hesitated, then took it and climbed back.
That evening Mridul sat with Pradeep and his parents. "Saving the goat was brave. That was for the goat. Today was for their phones." Pradeep stared at the floor, then nodded slowly.

qa.q: What had Pradeep rescued from the river last year?
qa.a: A drowning goat, pulled out calmly with a rope.

qa.q: What did Mridul feel when he saw Pradeep on the bridge?
qa.a: Mridul felt a sick drop of fear, seeing Pradeep outside the railing with boys chanting and filming.

qa.q: What did Mridul do to keep Pradeep safe?
qa.a: He walked up quickly without shouting, got Pradeep to take his hand and climb back, and talked it through with his parents that evening.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see the difference Mridul pointed out?
qa.a: Pradeep seems to start seeing that the goat rescue served a real need, while the dare served an audience.

grounding: Shows an adult watching a teenager take a dangerous dare and telling it apart from real courage, which serves a value, not an audience.

passage:
Selin was scrolling on her lunch break in Istanbul when she saw it: a video from her niece Zeynep's class group, Zeynep halfway up the fence of a construction site at dusk, friends shouting, "Higher! Higher!" Over three hundred likes.
Selin's hands went cold. Zeynep was brave, she knew that; she had once stood up to a teacher who mocked a classmate. But in the video Zeynep kept glancing back at the camera, grinning at it.
Selin called Zeynep at once. "Are you safe? Where are you?" Zeynep was home, fine. Selin left work early, went over, and sat with Zeynep and her father that evening. Together they reported the open site gate to the building company.
"When you defended that classmate, who was it for?" Selin asked. "Her." "And the fence?" Zeynep was quiet. "The video," she admitted.

qa.q: How many likes did the video have?
qa.a: Over three hundred likes.

qa.q: What did Selin feel when she saw the video?
qa.a: Selin felt a cold fear, her hands going cold, seeing Zeynep climbing at dusk while friends shouted.

qa.q: What protective steps did Selin take that day?
qa.a: She called Zeynep at once to check she was safe, went over that evening to talk with Zeynep and her father, and reported the open gate.

qa.q: What did Zeynep come to see about the dare?
qa.a: Zeynep admitted the climb was for the video, unlike defending her classmate, which was for the classmate.

grounding: Shows an adult seeing a teenager's dangerous dare and helping her tell courage that serves a value from recklessness that serves an audience.

passage:
From the staffroom window, Usha, the PE teacher, saw a crowd gathering by the steep ramp at the school gate. Aditi, from Class 10, was on her bicycle at the top, hands off the handlebars, while her friends counted down with phones raised. The ramp ended at the main road.
Usha knew Aditi as the girl who had calmly pulled a small child away from a stray dog last month. This looked nothing like that. Aditi kept glancing at the phones.
Usha ran down, stood in front of the bike and put a hand on the handlebar. "Off, please. Now." Aditi got off, red-faced. The crowd melted away.
In the office Usha sat with her. "Last month you were brave for a small child. Who was today for?" Aditi picked at her nails. "For them, I guess." Usha called Aditi's mother before the last bell, and the principal had the ramp gate shut at break times.

qa.q: Where did the ramp end?
qa.a: At the main road.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as she watched from the staffroom window?
qa.a: Usha felt alarmed, seeing Aditi hands-free at the top of a ramp that ended at the main road, playing to the phones.

qa.q: What steps did Usha take that day to keep Aditi safe?
qa.a: She stopped the bike herself, talked with Aditi, called her mother before the last bell, and the principal had the ramp gate shut at break times.

qa.q: How did Aditi see the dare after talking with Usha?
qa.a: Aditi admitted it was for the watching friends, unlike pulling the child away from the dog.

grounding: Shows an adult watching a teenager's dangerous dare, telling bravery from need for approval, and stepping in the same day.

passage:
Dear Asif,

I'm writing this because last night I was too shaken to talk properly.

When your friends' video came to my phone and I saw you on the railing of the canal bridge, with all of them chanting, I felt my blood go cold. I drove there at once and brought you home. I called Riyaz's and Karan's parents last night so every family knows, and I'm speaking to your class teacher this morning. That part is done.

I've been trying to understand it. You're not a reckless boy. Last year you stood up to the bus conductor who was shouting at Fatima Aunty's son, alone, when nobody else did. That was brave. It served something you believed in.

Last night served an audience. Your friends' phones. Their chanting.

I'm not angry that you want to be seen. I'm angry that you nearly paid for it with your life. Let's talk tonight, just us.

Your Ammi, Nazia

qa.q: Where did Nazia see Asif in the video?
qa.a: Nazia saw Asif on the railing of the canal bridge.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she saw the video?
qa.a: Nazia felt terrified, blood going cold, and then angry that Asif had risked so much for a video.

qa.q: What protective steps did Nazia take, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Nazia brought Asif home at once, called the other boys' parents that night and planned to speak to the teacher, so the danger was stopped and other adults knew.

qa.q: What might Asif have been feeling on the railing?
qa.a: Asif was probably excited and eager for the friends' approval, caught up in their chanting and phones.

grounding: A parent watching a teenager take a dangerous dare contrasts courage that serves a value with recklessness that serves an audience.
